name: Austria

facts.religion: Catholic about 52%, Muslim about 8%, no religion about 22%

snapshot: Austerity in a recession left the centrist coalition deeply unpopular, with the far-right FPÖ polling near 34 percent and its leader Herbert Kickl far ahead as preferred chancellor.
culture: Vienna was the capital of the Habsburg empire and of classical music: Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven, Schubert and Strauss all worked there, and the New Year's Concert is watched worldwide. Coffee house culture is UNESCO-listed. Alpine skiing is a national passion. Austria remains militarily neutral, a status it adopted in 1955.
society: Austria is wealthy with a strong welfare state and social partnership between unions and employers. Its economy is closely tied to Germany's and has suffered from the industrial slump. Migration and asylum are central political issues. Vienna is consistently rated one of the world's most liveable cities, partly thanks to its huge social housing stock.
situation: In September 2024, Herbert Kickl's Freedom Party won an Austrian national election for the first time since its founding by former Nazis in the 1950s. Every other party had promised not to govern with him. Austria then spent five months proving how hard keeping that promise would be: centrist coalition talks collapsed, the conservatives briefly negotiated with Kickl, and those talks collapsed too. In March 2025, Christian Stocker, a little-known conservative who became chancellor almost by accident, formed a three-party coalition of the centre-right ÖVP, the Social Democrats and the liberal NEOS whose main shared purpose was keeping Kickl out (CIDOB).

2026 showed the cost of that bargain. To close a large budget deficit in a recession-hit economy tied to Germany's, the coalition passed an unpopular austerity package, and voters blamed it. By summer, polls had the FPÖ at around 34 percent and Stocker's ÖVP at 18 to 19; asked whom they would pick directly as chancellor, only 8 percent chose Stocker and 29 percent chose Kickl (Börse Express). Stocker went on a summer tour of the country trying to reconnect, while a business-chamber scandal in Vienna gave Kickl fresh material. Commentators argued Stocker's best hope was to make himself the anti-Trump candidate, since Kickl openly admires Trump and Viktor Orbán (Vol.at). That bet looked better after Orbán himself lost power in Hungary in April. The question hanging over Austria is whether a coalition built to block one man can govern well enough to stop him winning outright next time.
power: A federal parliamentary republic. The chancellor leads the government with the support of the 183-seat National Council, elected by proportional representation; the directly elected federal president, Alexander Van der Bellen, appoints the chancellor and can refuse to.
holders: Chancellor Christian Stocker (ÖVP), in a coalition with the SPÖ and NEOS.

eat: Sachertorte and apple strudel in a Viennese café
listen: Mozart, Schubert and the Strauss waltzes
Schlager and the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's concert
argue: Whether the far-right FPÖ will win power

story: The Habsburgs ruled from Vienna for over 600 years over a multinational empire. It collapsed in 1918, leaving a small German-speaking republic that Hitler annexed in 1938. After occupation by the Allies, Austria regained independence in 1955 as a neutral state and joined the EU in 1995.
timeline: The Ottoman siege of Vienna fails
